questions.stem: What type of reaction occurs between ethene and bromine?

options.text: Addition, with both bromine atoms adding across the double bond
options.explanation: The C=C opens, both atoms attach, and a single dibromoethane product forms.

options.text: Substitution, needing ultraviolet light
options.explanation: Substitution under UV is the alkane route; the alkene adds instead with no light needed.

options.text: Combustion, because bromine is reactive
options.explanation: Combustion burns in oxygen; bromine is not oxygen.

options.text: No reaction occurs at room temperature
options.explanation: The double bond reacts immediately, decolourising the bromine.

questions.stem: What product forms when bromine adds to ethene?

options.text: Dibromoethane, with one bromine on each carbon
options.explanation: C2H4Br2 carries one bromine per carbon across the opened double bond.

options.text: Bromoethane and hydrogen bromide
options.explanation: That pair would be a substitution pattern; no hydrogen leaves ethene here.

options.text: Ethanol and water
options.explanation: Oxygen compounds belong to other chemistry entirely.

options.text: Ethene and bromine unchanged
options.explanation: The addition is fast and complete at room temperature.

questions.stem: Why does no UV light condition appear in the alkene-bromine reaction?

options.text: Because the openable double bond reacts without any light trigger
options.explanation: The C=C provides the reactive handle that alkanes lack, so no UV initiation is needed.

options.text: Because UV light would stop the reaction
options.explanation: UV is simply unnecessary here, not an inhibitor.

options.text: Because bromine produces its own light
options.explanation: Bromine water is just orange; no self-illumination exists.

options.text: Because the reaction only happens in darkness
options.explanation: Light presence is irrelevant; the double bond does the work.

questions.stem: How many products leave an alkene-halogen addition reaction?

options.text: One, the dibromoalkane or equivalent dihalide
options.explanation: Everything that enters ends up inside the single addition product.

options.text: Two, as in the alkane substitution
options.explanation: Two products signal substitution; addition merges everything into one.

options.text: Three, one per bond broken
options.explanation: Only the double bond converts to singles; no third product appears.

options.text: It depends on the alkene chain length
options.explanation: Chain length changes the formula, never the single-product pattern.

questions.stem: Bromine is reacted with propene instead of ethene. What forms?

options.text: A dibromopropane, with bromines across the former double bond
options.explanation: Any alkene takes the same addition, so the three-carbon chain gains two bromines.

options.text: Nothing, because only ethene reacts
options.explanation: The note generalises the reaction to any alkene.

options.text: Dibromoethane, one carbon short
options.explanation: Atom conservation forbids losing the third carbon of propene.

options.text: Bromopropane plus hydrogen bromide
options.explanation: That single-bromo plus HBr pattern belongs to alkane substitution.

questions.stem: Give the product of the reaction between ethene and bromine.
questions.modelAnswer: The double bond opens and bromine adds across it to give dibromoethane, with one bromine atom on each of the two carbons.

questions.stem: State the type of reaction by which alkenes take atoms onto their double bond.
questions.modelAnswer: Alkenes undergo addition reactions, with atoms adding across the C=C double bond.

questions.stem: Explain why the addition of bromine to an alkene leaves exactly one organic product.
questions.modelAnswer: Both bromine atoms join the molecule, one bonding to each of the two carbons of the old double bond, so a single dibromoalkane molecule is the only product.

questions.stem: Chlorine is bubbled into liquid propene instead of bromine. Name the organic product formed.
questions.modelAnswer: The halogen adds across the C=C in the same way, giving dichloropropane with one chlorine on each double-bond carbon.

questions.stem: Why is bromine water used instead of pure bromine for the test?

options.text: Because it is safer and easier to handle than bromine
options.explanation: The note gives safety and ease of handling as the reasons for the aqueous form.

options.text: Because pure bromine cannot react with alkenes
options.explanation: Pure bromine reacts even faster; the water form is chosen for safety.

options.text: Because water is needed as a catalyst
options.explanation: Water is a solvent here, not a catalyst.

options.text: Because bromine is colourless on its own
options.explanation: Bromine is strongly coloured; that is where the test colour comes from.

questions.stem: What is observed when bromine water is shaken with hexane, an alkane?

options.text: The solution stays orange
options.explanation: With no C=C bond available, the bromine remains free in solution and coloured.

options.text: The solution decolourises immediately
options.explanation: Decolourising is the alkene outcome; the alkane cannot accept the bromine.

options.text: The mixture turns blue
options.explanation: No blue species forms in this test at any point.

options.text: The bromine water boils off
options.explanation: Gentle shaking causes no boiling; the observation is about colour.

questions.stem: Why does bromine water decolourise when added to an alkene?

options.text: The bromine atoms add across the C=C bond, leaving no free bromine in solution
options.explanation: Consumed bromine cannot colour the solution, so the orange fades away.

options.text: The alkene bleaches the water by dilution
options.explanation: Dilution does not consume the bromine; the addition reaction does.

options.text: The alkene burns the bromine away
options.explanation: Nothing burns; no oxygen or flame is involved.

options.text: The colour sinks to the bottom as a solid
options.explanation: The bromine becomes bonded into the organic molecule, not a precipitate.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon decolourises bromine water rapidly at room temperature. What does this show?

options.text: The hydrocarbon is an alkene with a C=C double bond
options.explanation: Rapid decolourising without UV is the signature of the unsaturated alkene.

options.text: The hydrocarbon is an alkane
options.explanation: Alkanes leave bromine water orange; only unsaturation decolourises it.

options.text: The hydrocarbon must contain oxygen
options.explanation: The test reads C=C unsaturation and says nothing about oxygen.

options.text: The sample must be heated before testing
options.explanation: The result already occurred at room temperature, which is the point of the test.

questions.stem: Why does the C=C bond make alkenes more reactive than alkanes towards bromine?

options.text: The double bond has high electron density that invites attack and can open
options.explanation: The exam hint ties alkene reactivity to the electron-rich, openable double bond.

options.text: Because alkenes are smaller molecules
options.explanation: Size is not the driver; the bonding is.

options.text: Because alkenes dissolve bromine water better
options.explanation: Solubility is not the chemistry; addition across C=C is.

options.text: Because alkanes repel bromine strongly
options.explanation: Alkanes do not repel bromine; they simply offer no bond to react with.

questions.stem: State the safety reason that makes bromine water the reagent of choice when testing for a C=C bond.
questions.modelAnswer: Bromine water is an orange solution that is safer to handle than bromine itself.

questions.stem: A few drops of bromine water are added to hexane and the tube is shaken. State the final colour of the mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: It stays orange, because the alkane offers no C=C bond for the bromine to add across.

questions.stem: Explain, in terms of the bromine present, why the orange colour fades when an alkene is shaken with bromine water.
questions.modelAnswer: The bromine atoms bond to the two carbons of the double bond, so no free bromine remains dissolved in the water and the orange colour disappears.

questions.stem: Two unlabelled bottles hold hexane and hexene. Describe how one shake-test with bromine water tells them apart.
questions.modelAnswer: Shake a little bromine water with each: the alkane leaves the mixture orange, while the alkene decolourises it as bromine adds across its C=C, so the tube that fades identifies hexene.
